title: Workers Don’t Want Bosses Knowing They Use AI—Even As They ‘BYOAI’ To Work
text:
CEOs are talking a lot about generative AI, calling it a transformative technology and hoping it will turbocharge productivity. Just one problem: Many workers, worried they’ll look replaceable, are afraid to admit they use it.
Just over half of employees who use AI at work—52%—say they’re reluctant to divulge they’re applying it to their most important tasks, and roughly the same number worry that using it on critical tasks in their job makes them look replaceable, according to the latest Work Trend Index from Microsoft and LinkedIn. Still, workers are clearly using the new tech: Some 75% of full-time office workers surveyed said they’re now using AI at work—up from 46% six months ago—and more than three-quarters are turning to their own tools rather than company-provided ones, a phenomenon Microsoft calls “BYOAI.”
The annual report, released Wednesday, draws from a survey of 31,000 full-time workers, as well as LinkedIn labor and hiring data and usage data Microsoft captures from customers using its software. While the survey was commissioned by Microsoft—which sells its Copilot AI tool and has a big stake in artificial intelligence firm OpenAI—it still offers a snapshot of how workers and companies are using generative AI and thinking about it as the tech shifts from shiny new object to a tool that’s quickly reshaping how work gets done.
“The first thing we really see in this report is that employees want AI at work and they're not waiting for companies to catch up,” says Colette Stallbaumer, who leads the company’s future of work and Microsoft 365 teams. “A lot of that’s unsanctioned use.”
This year marks the first time Microsoft has worked on the report with LinkedIn, which it acquired in 2016, and found a growing role for AI in both job titles and in what jobseekers and managers expect. The position of “head of AI,” the analysis found, has tripled over the past five years and grew by more than 28% last year. Meanwhile, LinkedIn has seen 142 times more members add AI skills to their profiles, the report says, while job posts that mention AI have seen applications grow 17% over the past two years compared to listings that don’t mention those skills.
By “AI skills,” neither LinkedIn—nor the people who add them to their profiles—are necessarily referring to highly technical machine learning skills. “We're so early in this that it's all just getting called AI skills,” says Aneesh Raman, a vice president and workforce expert at LinkedIn. “Understand what it is, and then really start playing around with it. You’ll realize it is not some highly technical skill set.”
The report also shares findings from Microsoft’s software users. Researchers designed a randomized, six-month trial of 60 customers across industries that it calls the “first mass-scale observation of 3,000 individuals” using AI at work without interventions. The big takeaway: Copilot users spend less time on email—they read 11% fewer messages and spent 4% less time on them, Microsoft says—and edited more documents in applications like Word or Excel. Interestingly, the trial found that some Copilot users spent more time in meetings—perhaps because they have more time to meet with colleagues due to efficiency—while others spent less time in them.
But the hesitancy the survey found about employees revealing they use AI puts numbers to a phenomenon that has concerned other executives and researchers. At some companies, employees may fear sharing they use ChatGPT or another AI chatbot because there’s a workplace policy against its use. But at many others, it’s more about a mindset shift away from employees being able to take credit for their work at a time when many are concerned about job security amid a shifting economy and a perceived threat of AI.
Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who studies AI, calls this “shadow IT.” Employees, he told Forbes in a recent interview, “know if they tell you about it, then maybe you’re not so impressed by all the amazing work they’re doing,” he says. “Everyone is trying to not show that they’ve automated their work.”
In his recent book, Co-Intelligence, Mollick writes that research shows people judge work differently when they know content has been produced by AI rather than a person. As a result, “much of the value of AI use comes from people not knowing you are using it,” he writes in his book, mentioning an unscientific social media poll he conducted where AI users said they don’t reveal they’re using it at least some of the time. “If someone has figured out how to automate 90 percent of a particular job, and they tell their boss, will the company fire 90 percent of their co-workers? Better not to speak up.”
As a result, businesses that want to reap efficiency from AI may want to spotlight workers who use it as a way to reassure them it’s valued, and add training to highlight that it’s an expected part of the job. Microsoft’s report finds that just 39% of people using AI say they’ve gotten training from their company. “Companies need to have a strategy [for AI]. They need to have a point of view,” says LinkedIn’s Raman. “This is change management at a whole new level.”

title: Molham Aref Creates RelationalAI As AI Coprocessor For Data Clouds
text:
Data scientists, engineers and managers having been working for the past 50 years at methodologies to gain better business insights from large stores of data. Despite advances in cloud data storage and computing power, creating intelligent applications to extract knowledge from data remain a challenge.
Molham Aref has been working to change that dynamic with the creation of RelationalAI.
Founded in 2017, the Berkley, California-based RelationalAI provides a cloud-based relational knowledge graph management system, with probabilistic processing, and declarative reasoning at scale to make developing data applications easier.
The company sits at the intersection of three mega trends in computing—relational data base systems, knowledge graph software and artificial intelligence that together represent over $1 trillion in market opportunity.
“The inspiration for RelationalAI came from having spent most of the last 30 years of my life helping build intelligent applications like credit card fraud detection, supply chain optimization, revenue management, merchandise planning, or wireless network optimization. Those are all examples of applications that required a combination of technologies, including technologies that today we would classify as AI or machine learning. There’s been a huge trend toward building more and more of these types of applications, and there just wasn’t the infrastructure that makes it easy,” says the company’s founder and CEO Molham Aref in an interview.
The key insight behind the company is moving semantics or knowledge or business logic, closer to the data. According to Aref, the closer you can get to the data, the more you can make it operate, interchangeably with the data—the more effective you can be, because you're reducing technology complexity and the complexity of the technology footprint.
“Relational AI is making it possible for people to represent knowledge or semantics or business logic relationally so that you can move all of that much closer to the data and leveraging the relational paradigm. And that's why we're going to market as a relational knowledge graph, where we're organizing data in the form of a graph represented by normalized relational databases,” says Aref.
As Aref sees it, Relational AI is a paradigm shift that has been emerging since the development of SQL and relational database management systems in the ‘70s, knowledge graph software and advancements in Cloud data storage—most notably the rise of Snowflake and its breakthrough data platform that combined a new SQL query engine with an architecture designed for the cloud, providing the functionality of an enterprise analytic database.
Ten years ago, Hadoop had supplanted relational databases. But along came Snowflake’s innovative cloud architecture that separated storage from compute that made relational databases possible again with big data.
In fact, RelationalAI has come to market as a Snowflake coprocessor, which comes as no surprise as former Snowflake CEO, long-time Microsoft executive and billionaire Bob Muglia is both an investor and board member for RelationalAI.
The seeds for RelationalAI also began some 10 years ago with advances in theoretical work and cloud computing. “Certainly, Snowflake establishing the sort of cloud native architecture was an important building block. But some of my colleagues also innovated in this area around new kinds of joint algorithms that make it possible to represent intelligent business logic, relationally, with new kinds of query optimizers, that take information you have about your business and use it to make your queries run faster,” says Aref.
It took Aref and his now 165 person team, most of whom are engineers and PhDs, some several years to develop the software before signing on a few consultative customers like AT&T and EY who were also willing to work with the company as it continued to build its platform. RelationalAI will unveil its fully commercial version of the platform that will be available for public preview at their next summit in June with its self-service version available shortly afterward.
Cristian Figueroa, Head of Network Science and Behavioral Modeling at Cash App had this to say about working with the company in an interview: “RelationalAI’s knowledge graph coprocessor enables my team to see patterns, identify customer needs, and better serve our customers. With RelationalAI, we can now do these sophisticated graph analyses within our Snowflake environment, saving us significant time and money. What used to be done in days, can now be done in minutes.”
According to Muglia, RelationalAI integrates seemlessly with the Snowflake SnowPark data mart, but it also was designed to work with any data cloud and in fact started life within the Azure environment.
Given its potentially paradigm-shifting technology, its relationship with Bob Muglia and Aref’s own successful history as an entrepreneur, the firm has attracted some $122 million in funding to date, with it’s most recent $75 million Series B round in 2022 led by Tiger Global with participation from Madrona Venture Group who led the firms’ 2021 Series A round, along with Addition and Menlo Ventures.
Aref was born in Beirut where his father studied at the American University of Beirut. After finishing his undergraduate and Master's there, he got a scholarship for his PhD in agriculture and soil chemistry and was hired by DuPont to represent them outside the US, and moved back to Beirut, where Aref was born. The family then moved from Beirut to Geneva, Cairo, Egypt, Athens and ultimately to DuPont’s headquarters in Wilmington, Delaware. Aref was 14 when they moved to the US and finished high school in Delaware.
He went to Georgia Tech to study electrical engineering, computer engineering, but took all of his electives in computer science. He got a summer job working on computer vision systems with AT&T in 1991. “They offered me a full time job. So at that point, I was in graduate school and I was very poor student. I thought I'll do this for a few years. I really like the work and I'll come back and finish my PhD later. But anyways, that never happened,” says Aref.
He would leave AT&T and had the good fortune to work for a series of software companies in Atlanta in the data space that became successful and IPOed like HMC and Retek that was spun out of HMC. “I had one job for nine years in Atlanta, not the kind of gig you normally associate with IPOs and got to be part of two IPOs that were very good. And so that early on in my career I had conviction about what we were doing,” says Aref.
Aref then began his entrepreneurial journey by starting his own companies in the early 2000s. One venture backed company went nowhere. And then he started Optima with $300,000 of outside capital and sold it to Ericsson for $400 million. Another data and analytics company he started, Predictix, was acquired by Info for $450 million. “I then really wanted the Silicon Valley experience. And so we moved here in 2018, and I wish I moved here 20 years ago because you meet people like Bob,” says Aref.
In an interview with Bob Muglia he offered his insights on RelationalAI and Molham Aref:
“I've been working with these guys for like, four years now. And there's nothing else like it in the market. Molham was working with top researchers around the world at over 20 universities to develop a whole new set of algorithms. And in the process they wrote like, over 300 papers to develop this new level of relational technology to take it to this next level to be able to handle the problems associated with graph. And in particular, this idea of a knowledge graph, which is becoming more and more important, particularly now that we have these large language models, because a knowledge graph can provide the means to define attributes of the business in a way that is understandable by humans, and is also understandable by these models.”
“You can now, by using these new algorithms, solve problems that are graph problems at really high scale, and do so in a way that is very complementary to the way that the SQL platforms like Snowflake work. By building on the Snowflake platform, there's just a huge base of customers, very sophisticated customers, who by and large, are solving hard problems. And they need this,” says Muglia.
As for the future? “We have a super scalable business model. We have a very compelling value proposition. We have deep Moats. I think you can build a very valuable company and a company that has a lot of impact. So really excited about giving it a go, and with people like Bob supporting us, coaching us, guiding us and investing in us, having seen this movie multiple times,” concludes Aref.

title: Council Post: AIOps And Observability: How IT Teams Can Find Time To Innovate
text:
Ali Siddiqui is Chief Product Officer for BMC.
The goal posts for digital transformation are moving as the rise of AI and other advancements put new pressure on IT teams to rapidly deploy new technologies. That pressure is coming at a time when IT departments are struggling to retain talent and resources continue to be constrained.
This situation has very real consequences for how IT professionals spend their day. The primary goal of the IT team is ensuring service availability and reliance. But too often, IT teams spend their time putting out fires and responding to emergencies rather than helping their organizations innovate.
AIOps, especially with GenAI, is gaining mainstream adoption to help IT teams get ahead. AIOps refers to the application of AI to IT operations, aiming to alleviate routine tasks and foster innovation. With that in mind, let’s explore three key AIOps capabilities enabling IT teams to move from a reactive to a proactive posture, reclaiming time for innovation.
Cutting Through Complexity And Getting To The Root Of The Problem
Modern IT teams are tasked with monitoring complex, hybrid environments, often relying on a vast array of tools. Among these, certain platforms stand out for their intuitive user experience, integrating applications, heuristics and workflows into a cohesive framework aimed at enhancing operational efficiency. Such systems are designed to be accessible even to less-skilled first-level operations teams, providing AI and machine-learning-driven insights that transform raw system data into actionable insights and recommendations.
There’s real value to be had in consolidating data sources and tools to enable sophisticated causal AI to get to the root cause of complex problems. Generative AI takes this even further, translating those causes into human-understandable summaries, offering solutions and proactive predictions while leveraging operational and service management and DevOps to save time for IT teams.
Detecting Anomalies, Changing Impact And Proactively Preventing Problems
Traditional monitoring tools often have a significant drawback: many only notify teams of issues once they have already occurred, leading to emergency troubleshooting, slower systems and potential shutdowns. Reactive approaches often don’t cut it in today’s environment when services are mission-critical. As systems grow in complexity, anticipating and addressing problems before they arise becomes crucial and is the goal of every CIO. Proactivity ensures business continuity, which should include change risk management impact (both scope and severity).
The ideal scenario involves being informed of issues before they affect operations rather than scrambling to mitigate their impact after the fact. This entails utilizing predictive AI capable of identifying capacity and resource issues, as well as potential service disruptions or declines, and implementing automated measures to resolve them.
Accelerating Automated Response And Remediation
The speed at which systems evolve often outpaces human monitoring and management. This has necessitated a shift toward advanced, enterprise-level tools equipped with machine learning capabilities. These tools are designed to process and analyze vast amounts of system data from complex IT environments, transform this data into actionable insights, and drive automated responses. This enables IT professionals to automate actions based on a comprehensive understanding of their systems' operations and their impact on business objectives.
By leveraging data analytics and automated actions, organizations can better optimize valuable IT resources, allowing them to prioritize tasks, value creation and innovation activities to increase potential business impact.
Laying A Foundation Amid Challenges
Given the sprawl and diversity of modern IT infrastructure, networks and applications, as well as the heterogeneity of the data the systems produce, machine learning models and artificial intelligence are often seen as necessities in the IT operations toolbox.
In this environment where IT operations teams are focused on KPIs like failure prediction, root cause analysis and mean-time-to-repair, the human mind can struggle to keep up with the volume and complexity of data fast enough to make a meaningful impact on these metrics. When organizations rely on manual, people-intensive processes to meet the metrics, they may find it difficult to cost-effectively scale and standardize their efforts.
However, many organizations will face challenges with implementing AIOps technologies. These challenges may include:
• Data Quality: IT teams need to constantly monitor and account for the millions of data sources ingested and ensure it’s free from errors and bias. Bad data can cause severe consequences such as misuse or flawed outputs.
• Complexity And Scale: As enterprises’ IT operations grow and data and tools increase, there’s the added challenge of reconciliation and service modeling of assets that span cloud to mainframe and application to network.
• Silos: IT organizations are often siloed off instead of being under a single umbrella.
• Automation Confidence: It can be difficult to get the right context for root cause isolation and recommended actions based on historical occurrences.
To successfully implement AIOps, it’s important to implement it with an open platform that integrates with existing tools, provides out-of-the-box advanced AI/ML (including causal, predictive and generative AI) and accelerates automation. Ultimately, you should think about the use cases that are important for your business and start small to prove the value. By taking this approach, AIOps can help you make better and faster decisions for your organization.
A solid AIOps strategy also requires a cultural change. Successful organizations standardize processes to simplify automation, improve governance to support new roles and effectively address organizational change management. In practice, this means ensuring internal goals are aligned, teams are prepared to embrace failure and grow from it, and cross-functional collaboration is happening. Open and consistent communication is essential. This cultural shift can ensure that employee resources are used effectively and that everyone is working toward a common company goal.
Overall, a strategic approach to AIOps can help streamline operations for IT teams. It lays a solid foundation for driving the automation of IT operations, helping the business innovate more rapidly.

title: Council Post: Conquering Linguistic Frontiers: How AI Can Enable Global Marketing
text:
Founder and CEO of the AI engine for Paid Search BrightBid.com.
Imagine a world where language and culture are not obstacles, but steppingstones to global marketing success.
This isn’t science fiction speculation; it could soon be our reality. A recent Quantumrun article forecasts that language differences will no longer be “a barrier between individuals and cultures” by 2031. Advancements in technologies like universal language translator earbuds or augmented reality glasses, they explain, could make real-time language translation and interpretation instantaneous.
2031 might seem far away but AI-powered natural language programming (NLP) models are rapidly evolving. For many years, the biggest issue with automated translation and localization tools was their inability to correctly channel the semantics from one language to another. AI is working to solve that problem.
Companies today are already using AI translation tools to penetrate new markets. AI can help ensure consistency in translations, maintaining a unified brand image across different markets and reducing errors. Looks like we are on a good pace making 2031 a reality.
The Role Of Borderless Marketing
Marketing and e-commerce will eventually become an integral part of this coming barrierless world. AI can help upscale sophisticated, multilevel marketing campaigns across different markets.
Generative AI allows companies to personalize users’ experiences, whether they are on a website or app, shopping online or reading a blog. By using AI to remove language and cultural borders, brands can speak directly to consumers across the globe, not just in different languages, but in the unique voices of each culture.
While initial setup costs exist, AI localization systems can offer long-term cost savings by handling large volumes of content. Continuous improvement through training AI tools can also allow the technology to stay agile and adapt to language trends or cultural shifts, ensuring relevance over time. With scalability, AI-driven solutions can also handle multiple languages and regions simultaneously, making it easier to expand into new markets.
Today, when entering a new market, AI can localize your messages, product propositions and CTAs and send out dozens or even hundreds of marketing campaigns right away. In fact, the localization industry powered by AI is expected to reach a value of $27.46 billion.
And it is not just about the market size of localization and translation services. Localized and geotargeted campaigns bring six times more engagement while unlocalized marketing content can result in 13% customer loss. The inability to localize marketing content swiftly may lead to the loss of market share because someone else armed with AI can handle these tasks much faster.
Challenges With AI-Based Localization
However, there are challenges to consider.
Machines aren’t perfect, so humans still need to check their work when it comes to translation accuracy and cultural nuances. In fact, 99% of companies use human oversight to check the results of AI translation. That’s why it’s important to train your staff on AI’s strengths and weaknesses.
Also, just like any system, AI needs to be compliant with how it processes data. To ensure full compliance with regulations when using AI localization tools, the AI tools must be trained regularly—the more high-quality data it is fed, the smarter and to the point the results of its job will be.
Like intrepid explorers, we have the tools and ingenuity to conquer new frontiers. And in the exciting expanse of global marketing, AI offers hope for a future where marketing transcends barriers, connecting people and brands in meaningful ways. Don’t just speak to the world. Engage in a rich dialogue, one that celebrates the tapestry of global cultures and brings value.

title: Council Post: Six Verification Challenges To Watch For In 2024
text:
Andrew Sever is the CEO of Sumsub, a full-cycle verification platform that secures the whole user journey.
AI and digitalization have boosted business growth, but they’re also posing new risks. I’ve already explained why know-your-customer (KYC) approaches alone can’t keep you safe anymore (spoiler: 70% of fraud activity occurs past the onboarding stage). This time, let’s take a closer look at the six most threatening fraud trends you should be aware of in 2024.
Six Most Threatening Fraud Trends
1. AI-Generated Fraud
According to the results of our internal research, published in Sumsub’s 2023 report, deepfakes increased over 10 times between 2022 and 2023. The most impacted regions were North America and Asia-Pacific, showing an increase of 1,740% and 1,530% respectively.
Rapidly growing AI fraud is leading to huge losses. Recently, a Hong Kong multinational lost over $25 million when AI was used to impersonate the company’s CFO. According to the police, this crime was pulled off using deepfake technology.
Unfortunately, we can expect more AI-generated fraud on the horizon. For example, the technology can be used to impersonate legitimate financial institutions, deceiving victims into sending payments to them. According to Visa, 1 in 3 consumers is a victim of such a scheme, called authorized push payment (APP) fraud. This scheme resulted in customers’ total losses of 239.3 million pounds (approximately $303 million) in the first half of 2023.
Regulators worldwide are confronting the spread of AI-generated fraud. The U.K. is developing its AI white paper, and the EU has recently passed the EU AI Act, to name just a couple.
2. Fake IDs
Generative AI technologies are also leading to an increase in forged identity documents, with fake IDs up by 163% in growing markets. Creating fake IDs is now easier than ever, with websites like OnlyFake that create believable fake IDs in minutes. These services are frighteningly cheap, which now means that anyone can create a fake ID in no time.
Moreover, fake IDs made on sites like OnlyFake are managing to fool KYC systems. A 404 Media article reported that an OnlyFake-generated ID passed verification at OKX, a crypto exchange. This is why it’s essential for companies to go beyond simple KYC checks, implementing advanced technologies that can spot AI-generated images throughout the customer life cycle.
3. Money Muling
Money muling is when criminals use other peoples’ legitimate banking credentials to launder illicit funds—and cases are on the rise. In 2023, Europol identified 10,759 money mules and 474 recruiters, totaling 100 million euros in reported losses. In the U.S., one person single-handedly managed to launder over $2.8 million over three years on behalf of a fraudster he met online.
We expect money muling cases to continue growing worldwide, with young people being especially vulnerable. According to U.K. nonprofit Cifas, 23% of reported money muling cases involved individuals under 21.
Still, there are ways that businesses can fight back against money muling. To start, consider risk-scoring applicants, analyzing users’ behavior and monitoring transactions.
4. Account Takeover
Sumsub’s internal statistics show that global account takeover cases grew by 155% in 2023. Just recently, Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen had his personal accounts hacked, leading to losses of $112 million. Luckily, Larsen spotted the takeover quickly and notified authorities. Often, however, the outcome can be even worse, with grim consequences across all industries.
There are two key contributing factors to increased account takeovers: human vulnerabilities (e.g., when a person actually believes a scammer and falls victim as a result) and weaknesses in platform ecosystems (e.g., absence of additional authentication checks), which allow criminals to steal virtually any account. To fight back, we need to widely implement multifactor authentication, biometric checks, login attempt limits, notifications to account owners over suspicious behavior and IP address monitoring.
5. Forced Verification
This is when someone goes through verification against their will. They may be unconscious (sleeping, for example) or physically forced to enter the platform under threat of violence. Although this scheme isn’t as widespread as the others, our internal statistics showed that, from 2022 to 2023, forced verification increased by 305%. These cases usually can be spotted through a liveness check—or by detecting suspicious background noises and atypical user behavior.
6. Fraud Networks
Also known as fraud rings, fraud networks are detected when there are interconnected groups of people who commit fraud together. Sumsub internal data shows that in 2023, an average of 1% of global users of digital platforms or services belonged to fraud networks. They may be found anywhere in the world, but regional differences are noticeable: In Europe and the Americas, the percentage of users involved in fraud networks is only 0.3%, whereas in Asia, it’s 2.6%. To spot fraud rings, businesses should use AI-driven methods of detecting suspicious user behavior, transactions and applicants’ connections.
Conclusion
Detecting fraudulent activities is a difficult task. That’s why companies need to secure the entire user journey instead of simply focusing on the onboarding stage. They should create comprehensive fraud prevention strategies that go beyond traditional KYC solutions. The complex approach has to consist of behavioral anti-fraud measures, transaction monitoring and support from a legal team. This should go hand in hand with providing regular employee training and employing advanced user authentication methods.
Moreover, companies should implement machine learning algorithms, which can analyze vast datasets and spot fraudulent activities where humans can’t. This way businesses will be able to fight AI-driven fraud by implementing AI-powered solutions, making it more difficult for fraudsters to bypass the security systems. If all of this gets implemented properly, securing the system from every angle, it’s more likely that fraudsters won’t be able to succeed in their endeavors.
